The promise to an account is simple: the right cases, on their day, inside their receiving window. Everything below protects it.
Find the account. Check the route day and the
Add the order with each item and the number of cases. The delivery date is their next route day.
Orders taken after 3 pm the day before a route go on the next route, unless the warehouse lead agrees.
If an item is out, say so now and offer what you have. Do not take an order you cannot fill.
The afternoon before the route, open
on the orders you pick, so two pickers never pick the same order.
Pick by aisle and bay. Always take the
; the lot code is on the case and the oldest is on the item row.
Count each order twice, wrap it, and label it with the account and the stop number.
Load in reverse stop order: the last stop goes in first. Keep cool items together near the door. Schools and senior living kitchens have the earliest windows, so they are usually first.
Arrive inside the account's receiving window. If you will be late, call the buyer before the window opens.
The buyer counts with you and signs the slip.
Cases short or damaged: write them on the slip, take a photo, and enter
Slips go to accounts the same day; invoices go out for what was delivered.
Damaged cases come back to the returns bay, not to the shelf.
Shorts are offered on the next route, or credited if the account prefers.

A missed delivery is called in by the driver before the end of the window, then by the order desk with a new time. A wrong item is collected on the next route and credited. Note what happened on the order, so the pattern shows if it happens again.
Running out disappoints an account. Overbuying ties up cash and risks out-of-date stock. Reorder points sit between the two.

Reorder point = cases sold in a normal week x (lead time in weeks) + safety stock. Example: penne sells about 20 cases a week. Harborline takes 9 days (1.3 weeks). 20 x 1.3 = 26, plus 4 cases of safety stock makes 30. Review every reorder point each quarter, and raise them before the holidays and back-to-school.
Group items by supplier. Use the reorder quantity on each item.
. If you are short of it, add slower items you will need within the month rather than paying a small-order fee.
Add the purchase order: what is on it, cases, goods total, freight, ordered today, expected today plus lead time.
Count cases against the purchase order before you sign the carrier's bill.
Check best-by dates. Refuse anything with less than half its shelf life left unless agreed in advance.
if the new stock is older than what is on the shelf (it rarely is).
every week. Offer those items to your biggest accounts first, as a deal if needed. Anything inside 14 days is pulled and donated to the food bank, with a note of the cases on the item page.
Freight is part of what an item costs you. When a purchase order arrives, divide the freight across the cases and check that
still reflects it. If freight has crept up, your margin has crept down.
You are carrying your accounts' stock on credit. Collecting on time is what keeps the trucks running.
Accounts runs a credit check: two trade references and a bank reference.
. New accounts start on Net 15 with a modest limit, or cash on delivery; raise it after three months of paying on time.

Accounts on Net terms get one invoice a week covering every delivery that week; cash-on-delivery accounts pay at the door. Orders under 300 dollars carry a 15 dollar delivery charge. Invoice what was delivered, not what was ordered, and write the sales order numbers in
. The due date follows the account's terms. Any short or damaged cases come off the invoice, or go on a
. A short, friendly reminder to each account two days before the due date saves most chasing.
. Send a reminder the day after the due date and add one to
At two reminders, call the buyer. Ask when, not if, and note the promise on the invoice.
When money arrives, set the invoice to
, with the date and how they paid.
: nothing overdue and under the limit.
: something is overdue. The order desk mentions it politely when the next order comes in.
: what is owed is above the credit limit. New orders wait until accounts clears them. Tell the buyer before the route, never at the door.
On the first of the month, send every account a statement of open invoices. Many businesses pay from statements, not invoices.

After 60 days overdue, the owner calls. Agree a payment plan in writing and move the account to cash on delivery until it is cleared. After 90 days, stop deliveries. It is better to lose an account that will not pay than to keep delivering to it.
